    <id>https://noahmickel.com/notes-on-overconsumption-and-instead-of-a-self-help-book/</id>
    <title>notes on overconsumption and instead of a self help book</title>
    <updated>2026-07-28T20:29:24.065250+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>noahmickel</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;I had an acquaintance explain to me that his current income of $200,000 a year salary is insufficient to travel whenever he wants, let alone purchase all the luxuries (two mansions, a Bugatti, a supermodel wife) he needs to be happy. This is a truly sad (let alone misogynistic) perspective on life, but it's a hyperbolic version of the typical argument for every product in modern American capitalism. "Buy my product and you'll feel &lt;x&gt;" is the pitch for every sports car or phone upgrade.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The pathetic nature of luxury overconsumption does not seem to extend, however, into the kinds of things that people assume "make us better." Friends may give sideeye to a 29-year-old when they lease an Audi they can't afford, but the same is not necessarily true for dubious supplements, self-help books, or overprescriptive planning tools. Only in America can multinational companies explain to people that their true self-actualization will only arise via the purchase additional consumer goods.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I will not rewrite here all the work of Peter and Michael over on "If Books Could Kill", but needless to say the self-help book is an incredible example of how someone can take semi-useful advice and bloat it up to book length. In lieu of every self help book you could purchase, here is a brief list of things that makes my life better than it used to be.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h1 id=instead-of-a-self-help-book-by-a-man-too-busy-to-write-one-and-frankly-couldnt-be-bothered&gt;Instead of a Self-Help Book by A Man Too Busy to Write One (and frankly couldn't be bothered)&lt;/h1&gt;&lt;h3 id=1-find-a-job-thats-tolerable&gt;1. Find a Job that's Tolerable&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Finding a job that is within a reasonable number of hours that pays the bills is lexically prior to anything a productivity or wellness grifter could sell. Financial precarity under late neofeudalism is no joke, and until basic needs are met, no special secret productivity tool will cure longing. A company does not love its employees, and looking for cosmic meaning and justice from employment is a fool's errand. The same logic applies to the overworked finance bros, who should get a real job that isn't ruining the country and allows time for non-work pursuits.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h3 id=2-actually-care-for-yourself&gt;2. Actually Care for Yourself&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Drink sufficient water. Consume plenty of protein. Eat Vegetables. Take a one-a-day. Sleep 7-9 hours a night. Drink sparingly. Get exercise.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Wine nights, gratitude journals, and ice cream dinner (because "I deserve it") are at least orthogonal if not counterproductive to the simple shit. I spent too much of my life fantastically overweight, and decided I didn't want to treat myself all the way into adult diabetes. Probably widely applicable advice.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h3 id=3-do-things-offline&gt;3. Do Things Offline&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Read. Play board games. Host a cocktail party. Learn how to make good coffee at home. Woodwork.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The specific hobby is irrelevant, so much as it is disconnected from the internet. The real-world is lovely, go do something in it.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h3 id=4-buy-less-shit&gt;4. Buy Less Shit&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;People get used to luxuries quickly and it is a pain to maintain piles of stuff. For more information, see &lt;a href='https://www.youhavetoomuchshit.com/'&gt;You Have Too Much Shit&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h3 id=5-be-good-to-others&gt;5. Be Good to Others&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Purely selfishly, it feels good to take care of other people. Take your friend out to lunch for their birthday. Give the homeless person some cash. Plan an event for your friends to get together. The guy who does things for others is awesome.&lt;/p&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://noahmickel.com/notes-on-overconsumption-and-instead-of-a-self-help-book/" rel="alternate"/>

  <entry>
    <id>https://chupacabra.bearblog.dev/i-want-to-leave-the-internet/</id>
    <title>I want to leave the internet</title>
    <updated>2026-07-29T03:17:22.691369+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>chupacabra</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;I want to leave the internet. This site, reddit, my banking app, the cloud service, Youtube, my music streaming app, my email, Whatsapp, iNaturalist, pornsites, Google Maps, OSMAnd, the local DOT app. I want to forget about VPN and DNS providers. Microsoft Teams, Outlook for work.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I don't want to leave the internet. Wikipedia, the learning side of Youtube, this site, informative websites, OSMAnd, iNaturalist. I want to stop spending my life in this hologram, even more now that it feels so fake and so capitalist. There are parts of it that are enjoyable and useful, and that somehow improve my living. I'm looking for balance. The internet is not a real place, why should I be in it everyday?&lt;/p&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://chupacabra.bearblog.dev/i-want-to-leave-the-internet/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-07-29T03:17:22.691369+00:00</published>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <id>https://catsandbirdsandstuff.com/why-i-left-wordpress-for-bearblog/</id>
    <title>Why I Left WordPress for BearBlog</title>
    <updated>2026-07-28T21:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>catsandbirdsandstuff</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;h3 id=or-how-i-bought-myself-some-digital-immortality&gt;Or: How I Bought Myself Some Digital Immortality&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/catsandbirdsandstuff/bearblog-1.webp" alt="A bear sitting at a desk typing on a computer. AI" /&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;&lt;strong&gt;This is a re-edited version of a post that first ran here in October 2025.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I’ve just migrated this entire site from WordPress to BearBlog. All 70 posts, every image, every internal link. It took days of work, a DNS switchover that made me nervous, and one epic late-night session where I said “bedtime” and then stayed up fixing links for another few hours instead.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Was it worth it?&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Absolutely.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Let me be clear from the start: Cloudways, my hosting provider, was fine. About $15 a month for 1GB of space and an email address. Fast, reliable, no complaints once I’d got it set up. The problem wasn’t the host.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The problem was WordPress itself.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;WordPress is bloated. It’s slow. It’s complicated. It tries to be everything to everyone: a blog, an e-commerce platform, a membership site, a portfolio, a forum, a bloody spaceship if you install the right plugins. For someone who just wants to write stories and publish them on the internet, it’s like buying a Swiss Army knife with 47 attachments when all you needed was a blade.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The interface is a maze of menus, settings, widgets, plugins, themes, customisers, and options I never asked for and will never use. Every time I logged in, there were updates. Plugin updates, theme updates, WordPress core updates. Each one a potential point of failure, a security risk, another thing to manage.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;And the plugins. Christ, the plugins.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Want a contact form? Plugin. Want to speed up your site? Plugin. Want to manage images? Plugin. Want to stop spam? Plugin. Want analytics? Plugin. Want SEO? Plugin.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Before you know it, you’ve got fifteen plugins doing fifteen different things, all competing for resources, all wanting to track something, and all adding their own bloat to your site.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;But here’s what really got to me: the ethos.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Modern WordPress has become a tool for “content creators” building “audience funnels”. Every plugin wants you to capture email addresses, track user behaviour, optimise conversions, and analyse engagement metrics.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Pop-ups everywhere.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;“Subscribe to our newsletter!”&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;“Don’t miss out!”&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;“We value your privacy!”&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;All while installing 47 tracking scripts in the background.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The whole ecosystem is designed around monetisation, growth hacking, and turning readers into “leads”.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I don’t want leads. I want readers.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I don’t want to track people. I don’t want to know which posts they clicked on, how long they stayed, or whether they scrolled to the bottom. I don’t want their email addresses unless they genuinely want to give them to me. I don’t want pop-ups begging them to subscribe the second they move their mouse towards the edge of the screen.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I just want to write stories and let people read them in peace.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Here’s the thing that really made the decision for me, though: this blog isn’t just for now. It’s for later.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I’m seventy years old. I started this site as a memoir for my daughter Jennifer, a record of a life that’s been anything but ordinary. Stories from growing up poor in 1950s Swansea, my time in the Army, and the things we didn’t talk about back then but can talk about now.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The whole point is that these stories outlive me. That Jennifer can show them to her children, and perhaps her grandchildren one day. That there is a record of where we came from, even after I’m gone and my brain has turned to porridge.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;With WordPress and Cloudways, that meant paying $15 a month. Forever.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Or rather, until someone stops paying, at which point the whole thing disappears into the digital void.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Fifteen dollars a month doesn’t sound like much, but $15 a month for ten years is $1,800. For twenty years, it is $3,600. And that is assuming the price doesn’t go up, which it inevitably will.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;More importantly, it means someone, probably Jennifer, has to remember to keep paying that bill year after year, decade after decade, long after I’m dead.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Miss one payment, and the stories are gone.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;BearBlog is run by a bloke called Herman Martinus. He offers something almost unheard of in the world of web hosting: a lifetime subscription.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;About $200. One payment. Permanent hosting.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;No monthly bills. No annual renewals. No worrying about whether someone will remember to pay the invoice in 2035 or 2045. Just a one-time payment, and the blog stays online for as long as BearBlog exists.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Could BearBlog shut down one day? Of course. Nothing lasts forever.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;But at least the risk is not that someone forgot to pay the monthly bill. It is simply the normal risk of any platform eventually closing, which exists whether you are paying monthly or not.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;For something designed to outlive me, that makes all the difference.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Well, that and the domain fee. Jennifer will still need to remember to renew that every year, but it is about a tenner. Much easier to remember than a monthly hosting bill.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Beyond the lifetime deal, BearBlog, which could just as easily be called “Bare” Blog, does exactly one thing: it lets you write and publish blog posts.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;That’s it.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;No plugins. No themes marketplace. No widgets. No sprawling analytics suite. No email-capture machinery trying to turn every visitor into a lead.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;There is a simple analytics dashboard, but it tells you only what is useful: page views, unique visitors, referring sites, countries, and browsers. Enough to know whether anyone is reading, without watching them wander around the site like lab mice.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;BearBlog also has a discovery feed, and judging by how many new posts appear there every hour, a surprisingly active community of people still doing the old-fashioned thing: writing something and publishing it.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Just writing. Just reading. Just enough information to know that the reading is actually happening.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;There is a basic CSS editor if you want to customise the look, but you do not need to touch it if you do not want to. The whole platform is built around the idea that blogging should be simple, fast, and free of bullshit.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;And here is the best part: no tracking, no cookies, no surveillance.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;My footer now says:&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;blockquote&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;&lt;strong&gt;This site uses no cookies and collects no personal data.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;/blockquote&gt;
&lt;p&gt;That is not just a technical statement. It is a statement of values.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;It also feels like a small vote for an internet where people can read something without being tracked, funnelled, prompted, or converted.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Moving 70 posts was not trivial. I had to copy and paste everything from WordPress, clean up the inevitable WordPress markup cruft, migrate and rehost all the images, fix more than a hundred internal links that were hardcoded to the old domain, switch the DNS from Cloudways to BearBlog, and then wait for propagation while nervously refreshing the site.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;There was a moment, around 2am, halfway through fixing internal links, when I wondered whether I had made a terrible mistake.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Then the site went live.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Clean. Fast. Simple.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;No plugins. No pop-ups. No bullshit.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Google was already indexing it within days. Page speed score: 99 out of 100.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;WordPress never came close to that.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I’m not a “content creator”. I’m not building a “personal brand”. I’m not trying to “scale my audience” or “optimise my funnel”.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I’m a seventy-year-old bloke from Swansea who has some stories to tell before his brain turns to porridge, and I want those stories to still be here when I’m not.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;WordPress wanted $15 a month, forever, plus all the surveillance-capitalism baggage that came with it.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;BearBlog wanted $200, once.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;For that, those stories have a fighting chance of outliving me.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Simple. Fast. Honest. Permanent, ish.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Just writing. Just reading. Just stories that last.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;That is all it needs to be.&lt;/p&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://catsandbirdsandstuff.com/why-i-left-wordpress-for-bearblog/" rel="alternate"/>

    <title>Keep posting.</title>
    <updated>2026-07-27T21:45:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>bx</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Keep posting if you have something to say.&lt;br /&gt;
Keep posting if you don’t know what to say.&lt;br /&gt;
Keep posting if you agree with something.&lt;br /&gt;
Keep posting if you disagree with something.&lt;br /&gt;
Keep posting if it makes you happy.&lt;br /&gt;
Keep posting if it makes you feel insecure.&lt;br /&gt;
Keep posting if you want to have a discussion.&lt;br /&gt;
Keep posting if you don’t want to have a discussion.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I guess what I’m trying to say is, keep posting. There’s room for all of us.&lt;/p&gt;
</content>

  <entry>
    <id>https://livingkindfully.bearblog.dev/your-hell-is-someones-heaven/</id>
    <title>Your Hell is Someone's Heaven</title>
    <updated>2026-07-27T16:13:53.468522+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>livingkindfully</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Today I visited a refugee school that house 96 students. It is located in the poorer parts of the city. The school is right on top of a restaurant. They took about 3 floors.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;When I walked up the stairs to the school, the first thing it hit me was the smell. It is a unique smell that I could not describe. It is unpleasant. The doors to the school were mechanically locked and I have to take off my shoes to enter.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;There were wiring all over the place and the walls are due for a good coat of paint. As I observed from the classroom door, the students are happy and eager to learn. They have to wear their traditional school costume to attend the classes. Before each class starts, the student has to meditate for about 5 minutes. All the teachers are volunteers, some teachers are local and some are from their home country.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I sat down and talked to the head teacher. He told me some stories of these refugees. All the kids have parents, but the parents are busy working either in restaurant or rubber tapping in the Northen states of Malaysia.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I asked for a list of resources that they need. All the items that they need are things that we all take for granted. They urgently need a water filter system, cough medicine and fever medicine. Other items such as single lined exercise books, marker pens, washing powder, sanitary pads etc are also short in supply.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The school is being supported by the refugee's parents and also receive small amounts of help from the nearby Buddhist temples.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;As I look around the school, I wondered what future lies for these children. They are learning to speak their local language, English, Mandarin, Malay, Math and Science. They were all excited to see me and wanted to practise their English with me. They speak surprisingly well.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The living condition is poor by local standard. Yet, everyone carries a smile and look hopeful. This place is my definition of hell, but it is these people's heaven. A place that they can stay and escape prosecution.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The school's main hall which also serve as the sleeping dorm for the male children sits three buddhas. As I look at the buddhas, I pray for the school and everyone. I do not know whether my prayers will be answered.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I made a commitment to the school that I will pay for the school's internet expenses for as long as the school is open. A friend asked why I would want to make such commitment? I told him that I made a private deal with the buddha. How would I know buddha will honour the deal? I will never know. The very least, I want to give a fighting chance for all the kids that I met today. These students have showed me what it means to be in heaven. It is a state of mind. It is about not giving up, not knowing when they can ever go back to their home country. Yet, they still carry that hope and smile to face life's uncertainty. That's bravely and that's heaven.&lt;/p&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://livingkindfully.bearblog.dev/your-hell-is-someones-heaven/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-07-27T16:13:53.468522+00:00</published>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <id>https://nate.spot/re-reconsidering-bearblog/</id>
    <title>Re: Reconsidering Bearblog</title>
    <updated>2026-07-28T15:35:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>naheller</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Note: This is a rather spicy topic to do my JulyReply on, but there you go. This is just my personal take and nothing more.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;In reply to &lt;a href='https://scholarch.bearblog.dev/reconsidering-bearblog-or-on-the-value-of-words-new/'&gt;this post&lt;/a&gt;:&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I'm relatively new here, but I've been surfing the discover feed for a while now. Both Scholarch's and Absurd Pirate's posts about &lt;a href='https://absurdpirate.bearblog.dev/your-metablogging-is-lame-as-hell/'&gt;meta-blogging&lt;/a&gt; and &lt;a href='https://scholarch.bearblog.dev/re-blank-blogging-counts-too/'&gt;repetitive content&lt;/a&gt; struck me as refreshingly honest and important. Important because I think any healthy community needs its critics, especially those who believe in the core tenets and express themselves in good faith.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Overall I do see a good spread of topics and opinions in the discover feed, but there are always going to be some folks who command a bigger audience, float to the top more consistently, and therefore seem to set the tone for the platform as a whole. That's what we're seeing now.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Almost every meta-blogging post from these high profile folks seems to gain traction. The topic is easy to relate to because that's we're all here. It's easy to upvote because it's almost uniformly warm, fuzzy, and uncontroversial. There's a reason self-help books sell well, despite mostly rehashing the same handful of ideas. For some of us, it feels good to be reassured about things we've absorbed intellectually, but maybe not emotionally.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;For others it's like, yes, I get it, I'm special and worthwhile and there's no wrong answer and we're all in this together. It can seem sickly sweet. But if that's the message that some folks choose to focus on, more power to them. Whether or not some posts are designed to play to an algorithm, I don't know.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;But I do know that when we choose to publish our thoughts online for other to read, we are choosing to invite discourse. And discourse - especially the critical variety that makes us blush a little - is a sign that people care enough a platform to have strong opinions about it.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;From what I've seen, the back-and-forth between the folks carrying out this latest collective introspection has been respectful. Maybe a little spicy, maybe a little salty, but we're adults here. We can handle it.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;So how do we balance the sugary sweetness of "kindness and respect" with a mindful dash of salt?&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Well, &lt;em&gt;we&lt;/em&gt; don't.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;As Scholarch has discovered, this is not a democracy. We're at the mercy of a benevolent dictator. And Bear's &lt;a href='https://docs.bearblog.dev/code-of-conduct/'&gt;Code of Conduct&lt;/a&gt; is quite clear in showing the extent to which moderation is a subjective exercise. As far as I can tell, it's also a solitary one (correct me if I'm wrong). Which bullet point might Scholarch have violated in this case? Hard to say.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;What's clear is that our content's continued existence, or at least exposure, on this platform is subject to rules that enjoy a generous degree of wiggle room. That means ambiguity. And how could it be any other way, with such a small team in charge? To build an exhaustive rubric for every possible moderation decision would be a full-time job by itself.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;This is the price we pay (besides the subscription fee, that is), to use this platform and be promoted on its feed. It's the agreement we made the moment we signed up. And unless we host our own infrastructure down to the metal, there will always be someone else making these types of decisions.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;A big part of Bear's appeal is the discover feed and access to eyeballs it provides. But it really is just a privilege to be there. I guess you could consider Herman's personal interpretation of the Code of Conduct as part of the algorithm. So far I haven't heard of anyone engage in good faith being totally wiped from the platform. But you never know.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;So far I've seen much more good than bad here, and I really do want to see Bear host a variety of opinions and tough (but fair) conversations. I hope Scholarch and the other folks involved feel able to say exactly what they want to say, and to be able to "spar" a bit with anyone who's take a critical interest in their work. I hope Herman fosters an environment where this continues to be possible.&lt;/p&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://nate.spot/re-reconsidering-bearblog/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-07-28T15:35:00+00:00</published>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <id>https://actualspine.bearblog.dev/bearblog-is-not-social-media/</id>
    <title>bearblog is not a social media</title>
    <updated>2026-07-27T06:45:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>actualspine</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;That's it. That's my post.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Just finding it strange that social media expectations are still being brought around here.
Personally, I enjoy the quiet and people minding their own business. Finding well-designed or well-written blogs are nice bonuses when I feel like it.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Mostly, though, I enjoy tweaking with my blog's designs and writing my own stuff more. I write things for me, but if people intentionally decide to read my entries that's nice too. Unlike in social medias, I don't have to write DNI or watch online discourses thrown to my "For You" page because my blog entries are only readable when you click on them. And I believe people have their own &lt;em&gt;autonomy&lt;/em&gt; to decide what they want to do.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Like in AO3, I'd say "don't like, don't read". So, what are you doing here?&lt;/p&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://actualspine.bearblog.dev/bearblog-is-not-social-media/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-07-27T06:45:00+00:00</published>
  </entry>

  <entry>
    <id>https://departure.blog/toast-button-post-tags/</id>
    <title>Hiding toast button based on post tags</title>
    <updated>2026-07-28T22:18:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>sylvia</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;I've been thinking about how to selectively &lt;a href='https://salforth.bearblog.dev/hiding-bear-blogs-upvote-form/'&gt;hide the toast button&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Yesterday I wondered: how do I hide the toast button on all my #weeknotes posts? After I figured it out, I wondered: how do I hide the toast button on all my posts except my #bearblog ones?&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I'm not sure I'll end up using this, but saving it here for future reference.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h2 id=tags-toast-button-html&gt;Tags / toast button HTML&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Since the HTML for the tags and the toast button are right next to each other, I can use the CSS &lt;a href='https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Selectors/Next-sibling_combinator'&gt;sibling combinator&lt;/a&gt; to target the tags + toast buttons I want to hide.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;div class="highlight"&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&amp;lt;p class=&amp;quot;tags&amp;quot;&amp;gt;
  &amp;lt;a rel=&amp;quot;nofollow&amp;quot; href=&amp;quot;/blog/?q=weeknotes&amp;quot;&amp;gt;#weeknotes&amp;lt;/a&amp;gt;
&amp;lt;/p&amp;gt;
&amp;lt;form id=&amp;quot;upvote-form&amp;quot; action=&amp;quot;/upvote/&amp;quot; method=&amp;quot;post&amp;quot; style=&amp;quot;display: inline&amp;quot;&amp;gt;
  ...   
&amp;lt;/form&amp;gt;
&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;/div&gt;
&lt;h2 id=css-targeting-tags&gt;CSS targeting tags&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;I target the tag through its URL, e.g., my #weeknotes tag has the URL &lt;code&gt;/blog/?q=weeknotes&lt;/code&gt;, so &lt;code&gt;weeknotes&lt;/code&gt; is what I would include in the CSS:&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;div class="highlight"&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;/* If post has #weeknotes tag, hide toast button */

p.tags:has(
  a[href*=&amp;quot;weeknotes&amp;quot;]
) + form#upvote-form {
  display: none !important;
}
&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;/div&gt;
&lt;p&gt;(I'm using &lt;code&gt;*=&lt;/code&gt; for matching, which means the URL &lt;em&gt;contains&lt;/em&gt; this term, e.g., &lt;code&gt;notes&lt;/code&gt; would include both &lt;code&gt;notes&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;weeknotes&lt;/code&gt;. If this is an issue, using the longer &lt;code&gt;q=notes&lt;/code&gt; will be more precise.)&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;More tags can be added in a comma-separated list too:&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;div class="highlight"&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;/* If post has any of these tags, hide toast button */

p.tags:has(
  a[href*=&amp;quot;tag1&amp;quot;],
  a[href*=&amp;quot;tag2&amp;quot;],
  a[href*=&amp;quot;tag3&amp;quot;]
) + form#upvote-form {
  display: none !important;
}
&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;/div&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The CSS can also be reversed:&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;div class="highlight"&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;/* If post does not have #bearblog tag, hide toast button */

p.tags:not(
  :has(
    a[href*=&amp;quot;bearblog&amp;quot;]
  )
) + form#upvote-form {
  display: none !important;
}
&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;/div&gt;
&lt;div class="highlight"&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;/* If post does not have any of these tags, hide toast button */

p.tags:not(
  :has(
    a[href*=&amp;quot;tag1&amp;quot;],
    a[href*=&amp;quot;tag2&amp;quot;],
    a[href*=&amp;quot;tag3&amp;quot;]
  )
) + form#upvote-form {
  display: none !important;
}
&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;/div&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://departure.blog/toast-button-post-tags/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-07-28T22:18:00+00:00</published>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <id>https://winther.sysctl.dk/reading-books-on-your-phone/</id>
    <title>Reading books on your phone</title>
    <updated>2026-07-26T11:57:41.194126+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>winther</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Being on vacation always reignites my motivation to read books. I mostly read on my Kindle, but during this vacation I read an entire book on my phone. Because the ebook library service we have only exists as an app. While I do like physical books, I am not overly attached to the medium of literature or text in general. Still, it is difficult to completely ignore the sort of stigma associated with reading (staring at) on your phone. Staring at your phone is, with at least some valid understandable reasons, becoming less than desirable. Many people say they want to decrease their screen time, we setup various blocking mechanisms (with varying results) and we are in general more critical of heavy smartphone usage. While it is easy to take a photo in the subway of everyone looking at their screens, and then get it viral on social media with a self-righteous post about how everyone are zombies - or the counter flashmob with a group of people coordinate to silently read physical books in public transport (both get plenty of engagement on social media), we don’t actually know what people are looking at. Yes, many are most likely scrolling through reels, but some may be reading a book, reading the newspaper, catching up on messages from their kid’s school or whatever. I heard a podcast where someone said she has started buying very small pocket books, so she can read those instead of reading on her phone in public due to this. Of course we shouldn’t really bother ourselves with other people think, and that is true to an extent, but I can’t completely ignore what kind of signals I am sending to my kids. Whether we like it or not, it does send different signals to your surroundings if you are sitting on the couch looking at your phone with high focus for half an hour or doing the same with a paper book.&lt;/p&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://winther.sysctl.dk/reading-books-on-your-phone/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-07-26T11:57:41.194126+00:00</published>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <id>https://folkmoss.bearblog.dev/the-dichotomy-of-blogging/</id>
    <title>The dichotomy of blogging</title>
    <updated>2026-07-25T20:22:19.877474+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>folkmoss</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p class="post-meta"&gt; Last edited 3 days, 14 hours ago. &lt;/p&gt; 
&lt;p&gt;First off, before anything else, I just wanted to give a big thanks to everyone who emailed me regarding my &lt;a href='/digital-entertainment-with-zero-money/'&gt;last post&lt;/a&gt; — people sharing their own struggles, or with tips for getting free stuff, or simply to say they appreciate the post/my writing. Thank you thank you thank you. It's incredibly heartwarming to read others!&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Now, having said that, it feels really weird when a post on this blog goes "viral". &lt;mark&gt;If I had a nickel for every time that happened, I'd have two nickels — which isn't a lot but it's weird that it happened twice.&lt;/mark&gt; And I guess that's the dichotomy of having a weblog. It's a log on the web, after all. For everyone to read. At least, this one is. But it's personal stuff. &lt;em&gt;My&lt;/em&gt; personal stuff. That, at the end of the day, I mostly write for myself, not others. &lt;strong&gt;I've never once started a blog thinking about becoming popular through it&lt;/strong&gt; (I'm not counting the time I started a newsletter on Substack as blogging, after all it was purely for professional reasons).&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;When I was a teen, I wrote to let the angst out and to connect with fellow angsty internet teens. We linked to each others' blogs and always left comments. It's funny thinking back, because I don't remember using RSS for blogs specifically, so I guess we'd always just keep commenting back and forth and visiting each others' web pages constantly. We didn't have a lot to do on the internet back then. lol First of all, there were no smartphones. All we had was a desktop computer. For me, I only had blogs, message boards, and ICQ. (For a little while I did use IRC, but it could get pretty scary; I met lots of creeps as a minor there and stopped logging in.)&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;And I'm starting to realize it's the same reason I created this blog — to share a few thoughts on the ether, to read others' thoughts and comment on them, to get a handful of comments back, maybe. To log my feels so I can go back and read them because now, more than ever, my memory sucks and I forget about my own life (thanks, covid).&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;What isn't the same, I guess, is the scale. Now as an adult on Bear Blog and on the general blogosphere, I don't have the same feeling of a tight-knit community of the same handful of people commenting on my stuff and vice-versa. There are &lt;em&gt;so many blogs&lt;/em&gt; on my RSS feed! So many interesting people posting all the time that I see on the Recent Posts feed, always new people popping up on the Trending Posts... And comment sections are not 'in' anymore. I mean, there are a few blogs that have one, but Bear itself and the blogging culture of the present is really discouraging of comment sections. I myself don't have one, I even disabled the guestbook (but that was bc of technical reasons). I guess we're now living through a phase of being completely burned out — traumatized? — by comment sections, but [old man voice] &lt;em&gt;back in my day&lt;/em&gt;, they were so precious and important. Also — now I blog in English. The anglophone internet is much wider than the lusophone one. &lt;em&gt;Especially&lt;/em&gt; on the indie web/blogosphere in the year of our lord jesus christ 2026.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;So yeah. I'm not sure if I had a clear point to all of this. I'm not complaining per se. Just sharing that it is pretty weird to have a random post hit Hacker News (?!) when all I do is vent on the internet expecting to be read by five people. Wild.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Writing this down tho, I'm reminded I gotta organize both my post roll and my blog roll. Eventually. Hopefully soon. But as a good ADHDer, not today.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;hr /&gt;
&lt;div class="post-nav"&gt; 
You can reply via &lt;a href="/contact"&gt;email&lt;/a&gt; or leave a message on my &lt;a href="/guestbook"&gt;guestbook&lt;/a&gt;. 
&lt;p&gt;⁂&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;⇠ &lt;a class="previous-post" href="/an-facinora" title="A.N. |  Facínora"&gt;Previous&lt;/a&gt; ·  ⇢&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;/div&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://folkmoss.bearblog.dev/the-dichotomy-of-blogging/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-07-25T20:22:19.877474+00:00</published>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <id>https://www.hardrefresh.life/things-i-want-to-actually-run-out-of/</id>
    <title>Things I Want to Actually Run Out Of</title>
    <updated>2026-07-28T05:15:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>hardrefresh</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;My last &lt;a href='hardrefresh.life/things-i-never-want-to-run-out-of' target='_blank'&gt;post&lt;/a&gt; was about things that I never want to run out of.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;And it got me thinking. Are there things that I would very much like to run out of, properly, all the way down to nothing, and never get to? Turns out there are. Here's the top five. And yes, there were more than five.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h3 id=the-hiss&gt;The Hiss&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/hardrefresh/deo-1.webp" alt="deo" /&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;You shake the can and you can hear it. There is liquid in there. Not a trace amount, an audible amount, sloshing about like it has somewhere better to be.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Then you press down and get a small polite hiss. Air. That is all that comes out now. The propellant is gone, and it has taken your ability to access anything with it.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;So you shake it again. Harder this time, as if the problem was enthusiasm. Same hiss. You do this three or four times before accepting that a can with liquid in it is going in the bin.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h3 id=the-long-roll&gt;The Long Roll&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/hardrefresh/toothpaste-2.webp" alt="toothpaste" /&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The toothpaste tube has stages.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;First the casual squeeze. Then the squeeze from the bottom, which feels like maturity. Then the roll, where you fold the end over and work it up the tube like you are wringing out a towel. Then the thumbnail, dragged along the seam with real force.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;By the end the tube is a flat, creased, silver thing. And there is still toothpaste in it. Not enough to brush with, maybe. Enough to know about. And it bugs me that I can't get to it using the conventional methods I've mentioned. I'd be lying if I said I hadn't cut open the tube. It was only a partially successful attempt.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h3 id=the-curve&gt;The Curve&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/hardrefresh/jam-2.webp" alt="jam" /&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Jam jars are designed by people who have never eaten jam.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The worst part is not the bottom. The worst part is the shoulder.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Just below the opening, the jar swells outward before it narrows into the neck. It sits there like a small inner tube. A ring of glass that is wider than the hole you have to reach through. Which means there is a band of jam around the inside of the jar, at eye level, that you can see perfectly and cannot get to.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;A knife is straight. You go in, you hit the underside of the shoulder, and the knife stops. You turn it sideways and scrape upward at an angle like a surgeon. You get about a third of it. The rest stays welded to the roof of the jar.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Then you look down and remember there is a second curve at the base doing exactly the same thing.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;So every jar I have ever finished has two rings of jam left in it. Top and bottom. In a low moment I have used my finger, assuming I can reach. It does not clear either one and it makes you feel like a bin chicken with fingers.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I would like a jar with straight sides and a square bottom. That is the whole request. Someone please make a jar that respects the shape of cutlery.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Technically this problem is not limited to jam jars. It applies to any jar with spreadable contents.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h3 id=ink-visible&gt;Ink, Visible&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/hardrefresh/ink.webp" alt="ink" /&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I like writing with pens. I mostly use gel or ballpoint pens. The ones with refills. The refill still has ink in it. You can see the ink. A good couple of millimetres of it, sitting in full view.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The pen does not write.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;So you begin the ritual. The scribble in the corner of the page. The harder scribble. The small hopeful circles. The diagonal scratching. The bit where you hold it at a different angle because maybe that is the problem. The bit where you warm the tip up on your hand, which I am fairly sure I invented and which has never once worked.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Then you throw away a pen that contains ink. This is the one that bothers me most, because the failure is so specific. Nothing ran out. A very small ball stopped rolling.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h3 id=sealed-shut&gt;Sealed Shut&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/hardrefresh/glue.webp" alt="glue" /&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Superglue is the only one on this list that defeats you while sitting completely still, doing nothing, in a drawer.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;You buy it for one job. The job takes forty seconds. Then you wipe the tip, you screw the cap back on properly, and you put it away feeling like a person who looks after his tools.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Three weeks later something else breaks. You go to the drawer. The tube is still heavy. There is clearly glue in there, most of it, because you used a drop. The cap will not turn. When it finally does, the nozzle has become a small solid rock with no hole in it.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;So you get a pin. You push the pin into the rock. Nothing. You cut the tip off with scissors, which is the last card you have, and either nothing comes out at all or the entire tube empties onto your hand at once. There is no version in between.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Then you throw away a nearly full tube of glue, buy another one, use it for forty seconds, and put it away carefully.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;None of these are real problems either.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;But there is a particular kind of irritation in being defeated by packaging. Not by running out. By not being allowed to finish. The product is there, you own it, and you are deprived of the satisfaction of using it completely.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The amount left is always small.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;It is also mine.&lt;/p&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://www.hardrefresh.life/things-i-want-to-actually-run-out-of/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-07-28T05:15:00+00:00</published>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <id>https://4s.bearblog.dev/bye-bye-bear-blog/</id>
    <title>Bye, bye, Bear Blog!</title>
    <updated>2026-07-27T22:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>4s</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Almost a year ago, I decided to give blogging a try. I thoroughly enjoyed researching and writing my posts (I put a &lt;strong&gt;lot&lt;/strong&gt; of effort into them), but seeing how little traction my writings got was usually disappointing.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href='https://4s.bearblog.dev/talking-to-another-species/'&gt;My best-appreciated blog post&lt;/a&gt; was very short; I suspect that was part of its appeal. What I consider to be &lt;a href='https://4s.bearblog.dev/hashing-is-not-encryption/'&gt;my best post&lt;/a&gt; was very niche, so I understand why it didn't get many upvotes.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;After that one, though, I tried to write about things that I expected to be appealing to a larger audience, but I always seemed to fail to reach them. I am either interested in things that other people don't care about, or I haven't figured out how to make those things interesting to them. Either way: life is finite, and you shouldn't spend much time on things that don't have a decent return on investment.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;As I wrote, I enjoyed the researching and writing, but if the enjoyment I get from those is the entire return, I might as well store my writings in an Obsidian vault and save myself the yearly 58 euro (incl. VAT) subscription to Bear Blog. 😉&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;In three weeks, on the 18th of August, my subscription will expire and that will be it for me. I would like to use this (probably last [1]) blog post to thank &lt;a href='https://khoaly.xyz/'&gt;Khoaly&lt;/a&gt; for their kind words. Without them, I probably would have considered the experiment a bit of a failure. Now, I don't.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Thank you!&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;blockquote&gt;
&lt;p&gt;EDIT: Several people suggested I should write without reader engagement in mind. The thing is, I don't write the same way when I know others will read it. If I'm writing only for myself, I'll research something until I'm satisfied and stop when it's "good enough." If I'm writing knowing someone else &lt;em&gt;might&lt;/em&gt; read it, I'll spend much more time researching, fact-checking, polishing, and revising. That's a much bigger investment. If only a handful of people end up reading the result (and that's perfectly understandable; I also hesitate before opening a very long post!), it's hard to justify putting in that extra effort. Since I have other hobbies I enjoy, like reading and programming, I'd rather spend my limited time on the ones that feel more rewarding.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;/blockquote&gt;
&lt;hr /&gt;
&lt;p&gt;[1] I still have three blog posts waiting but I don't expect to finish them within the remaining weeks.&lt;/p&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://4s.bearblog.dev/bye-bye-bear-blog/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-07-27T22:00:00+00:00</published>
  </entry>

    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Living in a small town sure has its drawbacks. The steno pool of suitors are almost non existent. God knows I’ve tried.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;It’s easy to fall in the trap of yearning for something your friends have. Life partner, baby, home. My own space is definitely on the horizon and I look forward to having somewhere I can spread my own wings however I want to.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Do I need a companion to be my best self? Nah. The beauty of having friends and family, maybe even colleagues, is that you’re never alone.&lt;/p&gt;

  <entry>
    <id>https://cherrysroom.bearblog.dev/my-presidential-platform-now-that-im-old-enough-to-run/</id>
    <title>my presidential platform now that i'm old enough to run</title>
    <updated>2026-07-25T21:14:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>cherrysroom</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;weather:&lt;/strong&gt; ☀️ slimy but hospitable &lt;br /&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;critters:&lt;/strong&gt; little blue damselfly, several swallowtails, many sulphurs and cabbages&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;hr /&gt;
&lt;p&gt;my birthday was over a month ago but, uh, better late than never. here's my presidential platform (besides universal healthcare debt forgiveness affordable housing public transit public education parks funding monopoly busting &amp;c. &amp;c., which every sane candidate will promote anyway). my vice president, should she accept, will be angelyne&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;anyone using those LED retinal hazards some dare call "headlights" will have said hazards destroyed with state-funded rocks&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;more vending machines and automats nationwide. this will have a whole cabinet position actually&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;all parks and public land agency workers will be authorized to fire paintballs at people who litter, play music without headphones, harass wildlife, or fail to leash their untrained dogs&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;because the private muskerberg entity has clearly failed in its duty to behave as a public square, all social media will be nationalized. its advertisements will teach vocabulary words, provide fun facts, and inform voters about upcoming elections&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;free straw hats for all tourists. some of you motherfuckers act like you're allergic to sunscreen&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;as it has clearly run its course, las vegas will be closed&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://cherrysroom.bearblog.dev/my-presidential-platform-now-that-im-old-enough-to-run/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-07-25T21:14:00+00:00</published>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <id>https://scholarch.bearblog.dev/reconsidering-bearblog-or-on-the-value-of-words-new/</id>
    <title>Reconsidering Bearblog; or, On the Value of Words</title>
    <updated>2026-07-26T23:41:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>scholarch</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Last Sunday, I wrote &lt;a href='https://scholarch.bearblog.dev/re-blank-blogging-counts-too/'&gt;a post calling out Robert Birming's repetitive writing&lt;/a&gt;. The post gained traction, receiving around 85 toasts before it got shadow-banned—removed from trending.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I'll admit it: I got salty over this.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Was it because the post was controversial? That it continued to receive toasts even after being hidden—and that I received a few supportive emails and guestbook entries—suggests that it wasn't a touchy or taboo subject.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Was it because the post was low in effort? Sure, it took about 15 minutes to make, and there's an element of hypocrisy in calling out low-effort posting through a low-effort post, but I've written short posts that are more trivial and less consequential (e.g., &lt;a href='https://scholarch.bearblog.dev/an-amusing-quote-on-information-overload/'&gt;responding to a quote when the quote is longer than my response&lt;/a&gt; or &lt;a href='https://scholarch.bearblog.dev/very-brief-notes-on-unicode-input/'&gt;jotting down unicode inputs&lt;/a&gt;).&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Was it because it was too harsh? I didn't go as far as to suggest Birming's writing was lame or the equivalent of AI slop (but see &lt;a href='https://absurdpirate.bearblog.dev/your-metablogging-is-lame-as-hell/'&gt;Absurd Pirate's effort&lt;/a&gt;), and my remarks were directed at Birming's writing, not his character. Often in criticism, discussions attempt to separate the artist from their art (or else discuss the pros and cons of doing so); the common reason is to focus on the quality of the art as a standalone experience (see &lt;a href='https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Death_of_the_Author'&gt;Barthes' famous essay&lt;/a&gt;). In contemporary culture, this separation is typically made so that problematic authors don't tarnish really good works of art (e.g., J.K. Rowling and Harry Potter). I posit that the art–artist separation serves the opposite function, too: we can critique subpar art without making it about the artist—which is what my recent post aimed to do.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;As I mulled over these thoughts (and pondered where my saltiness stemmed from), the realizations seeped in: the platform &lt;em&gt;thrives&lt;/em&gt; on meta-blogging posts; it is incentivized to maintain this production; and it will hide suggestions for alternatives. It doesn't really care for &lt;em&gt;what&lt;/em&gt; we write, but &lt;em&gt;that&lt;/em&gt; we write. That's the theme conveyed across no fewer than 14 posts by Birming alone since February 2026. Just write—even when you have nothing to say or don't feel like it.&lt;sup class="footnote-ref" id="fnref-1"&gt;&lt;a href="#fn-1"&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; It calls to my mind the image of a factory taskmaster. Produce, produce, produce...&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h2 id=what-i-am-here-for&gt;What I am here for?&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Consequently, I've been reconsidering my use of Bear. You see, I have that writer's vanity that all bloggers have at some level: I want my words to matter. Now when it is easier than ever to write and share words, I want mine to have value. This desire underscored the key message of my post last week:&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;blockquote&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Sometimes it's good to step away from the page or keyboard so that you can think and come up with ideas—preferably new and fresh ones.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;/blockquote&gt;
&lt;p&gt;In an ever-increasingly noisy world, I regard slowing down to ensure the validity, reliability, and quality of my thoughts as a good skill to develop. It’s an exercise in building confidence in my own ideas, while resisting the pressures to move fast and break things. If I have to say the same thing 14 different times to make a point, that’s not improving my writing, but cementing a particular template. I wouldn’t be blogging anymore; I’d just be adding to the noise.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I restarted blogging last December because I wanted to make sense of my life. I had the romantic idea that writing would be the key to saving my soul. I believed then (as I still do) that writing is a reflective process that enables and empowers me to have dialogue with myself, which in turn uncovers uncomfortable truths and difficult aspects that can be addressed to improve my life. I believed Bear was congruent with these beliefs: according to the &lt;a href='https://herman.bearblog.dev/manifesto/'&gt;Bear Manifesto&lt;/a&gt;, this platform gives me “a reliable, simple, and independent place to share [my] thoughts online.”&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Through blogging, I’ve reached a few milestones and epiphanies. I &lt;a href='https://scholarch.bearblog.dev/83-books/'&gt;let go of my attachment to physical books&lt;/a&gt; as a measure of my self-worth. I named &lt;a href='https://scholarch.bearblog.dev/fathering-myself-or-three-lessons-from-the-kitchen/'&gt;the shortcomings of my father&lt;/a&gt; and what I need to do to make up for that in terms of my personal development. I decided to &lt;a href='https://scholarch.bearblog.dev/quitting-reddit/'&gt;quit Reddit&lt;/a&gt; (and remain committed to that choice). And I found joy in having a space to talk about the music I was getting into for a while, when I was particularly susceptible to seasonal affective disorder.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Moreover, I’ve been inspired by the stories of others and how they make sense of their lives. In particular, I want to acknowledge:&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;a href='https://absurdpirate.bearblog.dev/'&gt;Absurd Pirate’s hot and humourous takes&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;a href='https://forsomeone.bearblog.dev/'&gt;Chloe’s unpolished, vulnerable, unapologetic reflections on being her parents’ caregiver&lt;/a&gt; (see also &lt;a href='https://fornoone.bearblog.dev/'&gt;her other blog&lt;/a&gt;)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;a href='https://folkmoss.bearblog.dev/chapters/'&gt;Folkmoss&lt;/a&gt; for the visual aesthetic of her blog and her thoughtful writings on how we consume media&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;a href='https://lauram.bearblog.dev/'&gt;Laura Michet’s&lt;/a&gt; slice of life adventures and commentary on video games (their design and in general)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;a href='https://toska.bearblog.dev/'&gt;Toska&lt;/a&gt; for writing about relationships and finding a sense of home (which have prompted me to think of my own journey)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I’ve also enjoyed correspondence with others via email. One highlight was getting &lt;a href='https://listeningroomsmusic.com/scholarch/'&gt;interviewed about my music tastes&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;In short, Bearblog has offered me more good than not during my time on this platform. This is why I challenge David Meissner’s &lt;a href='https://davidmeissner.com/blog/re-re-re-blank-blogging'&gt;characterization of my last post&lt;/a&gt;, as akin to “booing amateur musicians at an open mike night.” To work with the analogy, instead of booing, I was just looking around me, noticing that some musicians at this establishment seem to play similar songs and repeat their acts whenever they’re onstage. I was getting bored, and wondered if my fellow audience members felt the same way, and if/how we might have a more robust community setlist.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h2 id=next-steps&gt;Next steps&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;It sucks that I wrote this post with the assumption that it, too, will get shadow-banned. As a precaution I’ve started &lt;a href='https://scholarch.neocities.org/'&gt;a new site on Neocities&lt;/a&gt;. It’s a viable alternative: free, open source, no ads, supporter-funded, and free accounts can upload files and embed images. It’s also a bit more traditional with HTML and CSS setup, which allowed me to create a minimalist-gothic-manuscript aesthetic in an afternoon. I envision using this new site to continue working on myself, with pages that are edited over time (e.g., like Wikipedia articles) instead of blog posts (to minimize repeating myself).&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Yet I retain a need for blogging to express ideas, musings, and discoveries. What remains to be seen is whether this will be done through Bear, or integrated in my new site. The &lt;a href='https://herman.bearblog.dev/manifesto/'&gt;Bear Manifesto&lt;/a&gt; made a promise:&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;blockquote&gt;
&lt;p&gt;If you're tired of platforms that treat you like a product, welcome home. Bear is here to stay.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;/blockquote&gt;
&lt;p&gt;If Bear’s ability to stay relevant is based on faux enthusiasm for blogging, to the extent that remarks that draw attention to its artificial aspects gets hidden, then I have to conclude that I am, in fact, treated like a product.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I would like to be proven wrong on this front.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;section class="footnotes"&gt;
&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li id="fn-1"&gt;&lt;p&gt;This might explain the prevalence of meta-topics like AI and tech and digital minimalism—we all have opinions on these subjects, for by virtue of being on this platform we as a crowd are mindful of our relationships to big tech.&lt;a href="#fnref-1" class="footnote"&gt;&amp;#8617;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;
&lt;/section&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://scholarch.bearblog.dev/reconsidering-bearblog-or-on-the-value-of-words-new/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-07-26T23:41:00+00:00</published>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <id>https://fornoone.bearblog.dev/re-why-do-people-have-multiple-blogs/</id>
    <title>RE: Why do people have multiple blogs</title>
    <updated>2026-07-25T06:06:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>fornoone</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Jen writes about having two blogs in &lt;a href='https://jensgentledays.bearblog.dev/why-do-people-have-multiple-blogs/' target='_blank'&gt;Why Do People Have Multiple Blogs?&lt;/a&gt; after initially questioning why people would need so many.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I felt the same. On my &lt;a href='/for-no-one-origins/'&gt;old blogs&lt;/a&gt;, I'd write about anything and everything — having categories was enough. But that was years ago and our systems change over time, especially when we're coming back to something we haven't done in a long while.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I really resonated to what she wrote about trying to keep notes on paper:&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;blockquote&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I have tried keeping a paper journal to weekly agendas, notebooks, and the whole thing as I have an interest in collecting stationery items. Sadly, every single time, I lose interest fast or just… lose track entirely. I do still jot down ideas and notes on paper, but turning those thoughts into a full entry? That’s where it falls apart for me.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;/blockquote&gt;
&lt;p&gt;And what fell apart for me was keeping track of what was going on with my parents — more specifically my dad.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I spent years documenting every little detail of his day remotely on a Notion database I'd created. This thing was &lt;em&gt;thorough&lt;/em&gt; — I'd log wake times, bowel movements, when he ate, when he was given medicines and then system changed when I moved in. I was still logging it all but the care efforts were changing because I began advocating for him. My Notion database only grew more detailed and soon took over my days.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I had to let it go. I'd know his routine and his behaviors til they changed, then I'd adjust to those, and they'd change again. Dementia is a fucking horrible disease and after a while, the fatigue of keeping track of every little thing suddenly became purposeless. His doctor and visiting nurse never cared for what I logged, just a faint gist of behaviors would be good enough for them.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;After months of knowing this, I don't think I was &lt;em&gt;actually&lt;/em&gt; able to quit doing it until a few years later. It took therapy to get me to stop — which sounds silly but it felt like I was not doing my job and to be honest, I don't know what job I should be doing other than being my dad's daughter.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;After not logging anything and just basing the days off his behaviors — I'd gotten used to having that time to do other things I needed to do... because logging shit takes time.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;But shit was still hitting the fan. He was getting wilder, more out of control. My mom's also getting older and she's always got doctor's appointments lined up, plus she's fallen a bunch of times which always ended with me taking her to the ER. With both of them deteriorating, my urge to log all the things suddenly became an urge to just be able to say what I wanted to say about what went on that day. So I started a Substack.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;And I've already spoken about that previously. It wasn't a space for me and I unpublished all my posts just last month. I was at a loss on how to share my caregiver story because my first attempt felt so icky.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;When I joined Bear Blog, one of the things I remember thinking when I read you could manage up to 10 blogs on an upgraded account was: "Why would I need another blog!?" but then after tinkering with FOR NO ONE and still having my unscratched itch to talk about caregiving, I realized... I do need another blog. So I made &lt;a href='https://forsomeone.bearblog.dev/'&gt;For Someone&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;This blog is for me.
That blog is for my dad.&lt;/p&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://fornoone.bearblog.dev/re-why-do-people-have-multiple-blogs/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-07-25T06:06:00+00:00</published>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <id>https://piimyon.bearblog.dev/i-have-a-confession-to-make-i-check-the-upvote-number-every-now-and-then/</id>
    <title>I have a confession to make. I check the "upvote" number every now and then.</title>
    <updated>2026-07-25T03:17:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>piimyon</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;I have a confession to make: scroll to the bottom of the page. See that little button right there that points "up"? I would open up my blog every few hours and check the number right next to that arrow to see if it went up. Even by 1.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;When it does, I would feel this small spark of joy inside of me. And when it does not, well, I would come back after a few hours.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I crave attention as such. How pathetic. I think to myself. And yet, I can't help it. At least, I am catching myself when I am doing it. That's why I am writing about it. I want to feel seen.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;When did I start to crave so much attention? Must have been all these speech contests.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I have always enjoyed being under the spotlight as a kid. Something about others giving me their full attention for 3 minutes and listening to what I have to say satisfied my little ego. And so, the feedback loop has been formed since. I had always loved to stand on top of the stage to perform something, be it speech or a song. Deep down, I knew I was not confident. But someone gave me trophies for being seen as the best 5th grader speaker. Another trophy. A third one.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I kept wanting to be recognized as the best on stage, but I never wanted to work hard for it. You see, it just so happened that I was competing with a group of kids who were not great at speeches or singing. I got to stand out not purely because I was good at the time, but because others weren't that great.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;When others were great at what they were doing, yet I had to be in the same room competing with them, I shrunk. My confidence was out of the window and I no longer wanted any trophies. If it was something I had to work hard to get, I stopped because I lost interest.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;What exactly was I aiming for then? The trophies? The prize itself? Or was I trying to get attention? Was it the satisfaction that I get something anyways without having to work hard for it?&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Am I writing right now for myself? Or am I writing because I thought my writing would provide some value for others? Am I writing for the upvote button?&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;If I look at the blogging community and say: I want to gather your attention. Then there would be no difference between the 11-year-old me and me right now. I have not grown out of that child who wants attention just because. My ego is so tied up with numbers in my life: the scores I got, the number of likes on my social media post and the numbers in my bank account. At some point, I no longer would have to take tests, and I don't post much on social media anymore. But that craving, that desperate scream for attention never went away. It manifested itself under my very own eyes, and yet I cannot see it.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I have now made my confession: Yes, I want your upvotes because it makes me feel good about myself. But I am writing this to be open and honest about it. I want to tell the 11-year-old kid that is living inside of me: You made it this far writing about something that is true to your own feelings. And that is a brave act. It is so, even if the numbers indicate otherwise.&lt;/p&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://piimyon.bearblog.dev/i-have-a-confession-to-make-i-check-the-upvote-number-every-now-and-then/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-07-25T03:17:00+00:00</published>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <id>https://jottednotes.bearblog.dev/any-social-media-dyes-you/</id>
    <title>any social media dyes you</title>
    <updated>2026-07-27T04:15:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>jottednotes</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;maybe the title is a bit too strongly worded. After all, any experience effects you, changes you. You absorb knowledge, unique experiences, and derive your own thoughts. This is a normal human process, and you could even argue a normal living creature's process.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;But what about social media? you are not exploring, you are not deriving. Before you can fully think your own thoughts, another person's opinions appear before you. Maybe it's something you agree with, reinforcing what you already thought. Or maybe it's something you viscerally hate, sparking a response.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I've become more disillusioned in general to this process. That isn't saying I've disconnected from it entirely; after all, I'm still here. I browse my same old subreddits, scroll through twitter, or check up on what's going on on instagram. But its hard to avoid any kind of trends or communal opinions. Even bear's community clearly has a 'meta' - easily discerned from scanning discover for a bit.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;That's not to say this is necessarily a bad thing - social networks can entirely be organically driven. But I'm starting to feel more and more that using any kind of social network starts slowly coloring you - instead of your own discovery, you are now seeing through other's lens constantly.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;but is the solution to totally unplug? unlikely. The world is simply so connected now that the spread of these cultural colors&lt;sup class="footnote-ref" id="fnref-1"&gt;&lt;a href="#fn-1"&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; is not contained to the digital world - maybe people are simply blending more and more with their digital selves, a divide that used to exist, but these days seems to be rarer and rarer.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I think one thing you see more of now, as an act against simple consumption is the drive to create; the desire to be a entrepreneur, to be a content creator, to leave a mark of your own. but I don't feel that's the answer either; simply contributing to the problem instead, and getting stuck into a rat race of another kind.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;and surely the fix is not to only consume the 'classics' and become a hipster (even if not performative) - for the world is constantly spinning, and progress will continue, whether you want it to or not.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I guess I've just been feeling a bit lost lately. Not quite a crisis, but perhaps it's also to not having a pure purpose. I applied to a job that asked what my 'personal philosophy' was recently. It's a tapestry of what I've seen, and is any of it actually my own?&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;section class="footnotes"&gt;
&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li id="fn-1"&gt;&lt;p&gt;memes/memetics i think is what we can officially call them&lt;a href="#fnref-1" class="footnote"&gt;&amp;#8617;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;
&lt;/section&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://jottednotes.bearblog.dev/any-social-media-dyes-you/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-07-27T04:15:00+00:00</published>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <id>https://piimyon.bearblog.dev/who-would-ever-read-this/</id>
    <title>Who would ever read this?</title>
    <updated>2026-07-24T15:51:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>piimyon</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Who would ever read something no more than a mindless babble?&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I probably wouldn't. I am my own harshest critic. I think of my writings as mindless babble. They are. What value do they have for the world? Why would someone want to be interested in this?&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;And yet, I'd like to think that maybe someone would. Maybe someone does find this interesting.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;It is the need to feel connected after all. I do want to feel seen and recognized for what I do. And what do I have? Nothing but my mind and words.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;If I do not think of my own writing as something worth reading, why would someone else?&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I write anyway, to try to break out of my own shell. I write, so that some future version of myself can remember me a bit differently. I am so much more. I eat, drink, sleep. I love people and their lives. I wish them live long and prosper.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;But when it comes to my own life, I despise it. I look around and I feel disgusted. I get trapped in my own thoughts, waiting for someone to save me.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Looking back at these sentences, one pattern starts emerging: I. I keep talking about "I", myself. "I feel this way", "I think about that", and "I am doing this". I spend all my days being self-centered, wondering why I am feeling so utterly lonely.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Someone will be reading this. At least, future me will be reading this at some point. Sounds comforting to know that at least I still have myself to read my own writing.&lt;/p&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://piimyon.bearblog.dev/who-would-ever-read-this/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-07-24T15:51:00+00:00</published>
  </entry>
